thread.title: This ex-Leeds United manager has found success in India and Nepal. Now he's coming home
thread.title_full: This ex-Leeds United manager has found success in India and Nepal. Now he's coming home

author: Beren Cross
title: This ex-Leeds United manager has found success in India and Nepal. Now he's coming home
text: Simon Grayson was on the touchline as Lalitpur City's head coach in a dramatic play-off qualifier against rivals Dhangadhi in the Nepal Super League (NSL) and he had just watch his goalkeeper make an important save.But had the ball crossed the line in the process? With no VAR in the NSL, everyone had to trust the referee.What happened next was new, even for Grayson. He has managed for 20 years, take charge of nearly 800 matches, but never seen a situation like the one that unfolded inside Kathmandu's Dasharath Stadium."All of a sudden, I've seen this bloke walk down to the match commissioner's table (between the dugouts) and start talking to him," Grayson tells The Athletic, recalling the actions of who he believed to be an executive from the opposing team. "I look back to the pitch, then look back about 30 seconds later: this bloke's arguing with the match commissioner and rolling down the outside perimeter of the (athletics) track."Police are then coming down and you're like: 'What has just gone off here?' After the game, you find out that they were moaning to the match commissioner (that) the ball had crossed the line and starting to have a ruckus with him."Despite the controversy, Lalitpur prevailed that day and went on to win the final and, overall, the NSL, a month-long competition between seven teams in March and April 2025.The 56-year-old was only in Nepal for three months. Between June 2022 and December 2023, meanwhile, he was in charge of Bengaluru in the Indian Super League (ISL).In January of this year, Grayson was appointed as a board advisor at Cork City in the League of Ireland. Then, in March, he began working as an assistant coach under John Herdman on a part-time basis with the Indonesia national team.These are doors which have opened because of his long career in the English game. He started his managerial career with Blackpool in November 2005, and worked at eight more clubs in the English pyramid until October 2025, when Hartlepool United sacked him."I'm not saying I got jaded or anything, but over the last few years, I feel like certain people at clubs I've gone to work for, they've not fulfilled the promises they made that attracted me to their football club," he said. "Also, you get to a point where after 20 years and 800 games, you've done a lot and want to do something different, maybe."Grayson is speaking to The Athletic at Woodhall Sports Hub, a newly-developed £9.6million football facility in Leeds, where he is stepping into youth coaching. Simon Grayson Football Academy, which will coach all abilities between four-year-olds and 16-year-olds across three nights a week, is the latest of these new ventures he is pursuing.While he stops short of ruling out a return to professional club management, this is undoubtedly a new phase in Grayson's career. This step away from the treadmill of EFL football began with his move to India.Martin Bain, Sunderland's chief executive when Grayson was appointed in June 2017, was in charge of the ISL and invited him over to see the country and assess the league before the Covid pandemic wrecked those plans. Owen Coyle, the former Burnley and Bolton Wanderers manager, then asked Grayson if he would like to succeed him at Jamshedpur in 2022.While Grayson mulled it over, Bengaluru caught wind of his interest and swooped. Bengaluru, based in Bangalore, appealed more as a cosmopolitan city with an international airport and a more recent track record of success."After speaking to family, we said: 'Why not?' I live by the motto: 'You can only regret the things you don't do' and I thought if I'm going to work abroad, I'm going to do it now."Being outside of his comfort zone appealed to Grayson. He took Andy Beasley, his former goalkeeping coach at Leeds United, and Eric Kinder, a former Blackburn Rovers academy coach, with him."I landed two or three days before, and then you start coaching," he said. "I've got a big whiteboard to do my sessions on and I could tell, after a day or two, I've got to slow down. I'm in full Yorkshire twang, here."In his squad, Grayson had players from Serbia, Brazil, Australia and France, whose English was good enough, and then an Indian cohort, of which only three or four players struggled with the language barrier. He describes the facilities as League One level and more than good enough for the coaching he wanted to do.As he reflects on his time with Bengaluru, he recalls what he remembers being one of the biggest decisions of his career.Sunil Chhetri is an icon in Indian football. Only Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Iran's Ali Daei have scored more international goals than his 95 for India. Chhetri was in Grayson's Bengaluru team. The manager recalls opposition fans singing his name, such was his status.However, Grayson found that Chhetri was so influential, team-mates would pass to him even if he was marked by three opponents. It was harming the team and so Grayson dropped him."I said to myself, I said to my family: 'This is going to go one way or the other'," says the former Leeds boss. "I'm either going to mess it up and I'm coming home, or I'm going to get it right and be praised."Bengaluru won 10 matches on the spin between January and March 2023, and the gamble paid off for Grayson. Of the three trophies they contested, Bengaluru won one (the Durand Cup) and reached the final of both the ISL's play-offs and the AIFF Super Cup.In the first round of the play-offs, Grayson recalls an incident where opposition manager Ivan Vukomanovic was so incensed by a quickly taken Chhetri free kick in extra-time, which went in, he took his Kerala Blasters team off the field and refused to bring them back on. It ensured a spot in the semi-finals for Grayson's side.Grayson fully embraced his 18 months in India. He remembers taking at least 50 flights across the season for games or mini-breaks to places like Sri Lanka and Goa. His wife visited two or three times in that first season."I threw myself into what anybody wanted me to do," he said. "They dress you up with turbans and the gear on, and embrace what they expected you to do."It was an exciting period, but it also made you a little bit more humble about the surroundings people were in. In Bengaluru, (you went) from five-star hotels and restaurants to, around the corner, kids in poverty. You realised the discrepancies of that part of the world."Grayson and Bengaluru eventually parted ways in December 2023. It was the right time for him to come home.An agent who had seen his record in India eventually called him with the Lalitpur opportunity in early 2025. In Nepal, on his own without his recognised coaching staff, facilities were far more of a problem."The facilities were dreadful," he said. "For my first session, I had six balls and eight players. And then, even three days before the season started, I was waiting for the six foreign players to come in."They were all coming in from Africa, so, three days before the tournament started, I didn't have all my players."Despite the adversity, Grayson did steer Lalitpur to the NSL title in that month of games in Kathmandu. Although he was not there long, Grayson built a tight relationship with the staff, players and ownership there.It was hard for him to see the devastation caused to Nepal by the glacier collapse and flash floods in August."When you see that in any part of the world, it's horrible, but when it's in an area where you've worked, my first thing was to send a message out to (them)," he said. "We were all based in Kathmandu and it (disaster) was up on the border."These lads could have had families in that area where they're just coming down and my message was: 'Hopefully nobody's been involved in all this'. Fortunately, none of them were."Grayson remains in touch with the friends he made in Nepal and India. They are key parts of this latest phase in his career. He now hopes he can bring something new to his old stomping ground, Leeds, with a new academy for a new generation.This article originally appeared in The Athletic.
